title: Genesis 16. The Cup of Arrangement.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 16. The Cup of Arrangement.
Sarai, Abram's wife, bore him no children.
She has an Egyptian servant whose name is Hagar.
Ten years have passed since Abram entered Canaan.
Ten years since God said:
To your offspring I will give this land.
Ten years since Abram built altars and called on the name of the Lord.
Ten years since the stars were counted and the faith was reckoned as righteousness.
And Sarai is still barren.
Sarai speaks.
The Lord has restrained me from bearing.
Go in to my servant.
Perhaps I shall obtain children by her.
The Cup is filled, but not by God.
By arrangement.
Human strategy replacing divine promise.
The woman who was given the promise through her body now offers another body in her place.
The same pattern as Eden, abundance given, boundary set, boundary crossed.
But here the boundary is not a command.
It is timing.
God said offspring.
God did not say now.
Sarai cannot wait.
Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
The same phrase used in chapter three:
Adam listened to the voice of his wife.
The man who heard God's voice and believed is now the man who hears Sarai's voice and obeys.
The Cup that was received by faith in chapter fifteen is now seized by arrangement in chapter sixteen.
The vessel that was called righteous for believing God now follows his wife's strategy instead of God's promise.
Sarai takes Hagar, her Egyptian servant,
and gives her to Abram as a wife.
He goes in to Hagar.
She conceives.
And when she sees that she has conceived,
her mistress is despised in her eyes.
The Cup that was filled by arrangement does not hold peace.
The servant who was given becomes the woman who despises.
The womb that was borrowed produces pride.
The same pattern that will echo through all of Genesis,
Jacob's wives and their maidservants, the mandrakes, the rivalry, begins here.
The Cup of arrangement produces a child but not communion.
Sarai blames Abram: This wrong is your fault.
I gave my servant into your embrace,
and when she saw she had conceived, she despised me.
May the Lord judge between you and me.
The woman who arranged the union now condemns it.
The man who agreed to the plan now washes his hands of it.
Abram says: Your servant is in your hand.
Do to her what is good in your eyes.
The same abdication as Eden.
The man who was given responsibility for the woman now defers to the woman's judgment against another woman.
Abram does not protect Hagar.
He does not address what has been done.
He says: Do what you want.
Sarai deals harshly with her.
Hagar flees.
The Cup of arrangement produces a child, produces pride, produces blame,
produces harshness, produces flight.
The servant who was used to fill the promise is now driven into the wilderness by the woman who offered her.
The arrangement that was meant to build a family has destroyed one.
The Angel of the Lord finds her by a spring of water in the wilderness,
on the way to Shur.
He says: Hagar, Sarai's servant,
where have you come from and where are you going?
The same kind of question God asked in chapter three:
Where are you?
Not because He does not know.
Because the one who is lost needs to say it.
Hagar answers: I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.
The Angel says: Return to your mistress.
Submit yourself under her hands.
Then He speaks a promise: I will greatly multiply your offspring,
so that they cannot be counted for multitude.
You are with child and shall bear a son.
You shall call his name Ishmael,
because the Lord has heard your affliction.
Ishmael.
God hears.
The son born of arrangement is named by God: the Lord hears.
Not the Lord provides.
Not the Lord fulfills.
The Lord hears.
God did not plan this child.
But God heard the affliction of the woman caught in the plan.
The Cup that was filled by human will is met by a God who sees the one who was used in it.
He will be a wild donkey of a man.
His hand against everyone, and everyone's hand against him.
He shall dwell over against all his kinsmen.
The son of arrangement will live in tension.
The wild donkey, free, untamed, unable to be domesticated.
The child who was not the promise will become a people who stand over against the people of the promise.
The arrangement that was meant to produce the covenant offspring produces instead a brother who cannot rest beside his brother.
Then Hagar names God.
The only person in Scripture to give God a name: El Roi,
the God who sees me.
She says: Have I even stayed alive here after seeing Him?
No one else in Genesis names God.
Adam named the animals.
Abram builds altars and calls on the name of the Lord.
But Hagar, the Egyptian servant, the woman used in the arrangement,
the one who fled, is the one who names God.
And the name she gives is not about power.
Not about covenant.
Not about promise.
About seeing.
The God who sees me.
The well is called Beer-lahai roi,
the well of the Living One who sees me.
The God who was not consulted in the arrangement sees the woman who was caught in it.
The covenant was cut with Abram in chapter fifteen.
But in chapter sixteen, God meets the servant.
The promise passed through a man.
But God's seeing reached the woman the promise stepped on.
Hagar returns.
She bears a son.
Abram names him Ishmael.
Abram is eighty-six years old.
The Cup of arrangement has produced a son.
But not the son.
The promise still waits.
The covenant still stands.
The stars are still uncounted.
The woman who was barren is still barren.
And now there is a child in the house who was not the promise,
a wild donkey of a man,
a brother who will stand against his brothers, a son named God-hears,
born to a woman named God-sees.
The Cup was not filled by God.
But God saw what was poured into it.
And what God sees, He does not abandon.
